items.stem: A report shows average response time of 120 ms but users complain of slowness. Which metric best reveals the problem?

options.rationale: Correct: tail percentiles expose the slow experiences the average hides.
The mean is what already hid the problem.
Request count does not describe the slow experiences.
Uptime is unrelated to per-request latency distribution.

items.explanation: Correct: high-percentile (tail) latency surfaces the slow requests an average conceals.

items.stem: Which TWO test types are most appropriate to find a slow memory leak and to find behaviour beyond normal peak? (Select TWO)

options.text: A soak test for the slow memory leak
options.rationale: Correct: a long-duration soak test reveals leaks that only appear over time.

options.text: A stress test for behaviour beyond normal peak
options.rationale: Correct: stress testing pushes past expected peak to find the breaking point.

options.text: A single short smoke test for both
options.rationale: A short smoke test cannot reveal leaks or breaking points.

options.text: A static code review for both
options.rationale: A code review is not a performance test type.

items.explanation: Correct: soak tests find time-dependent leaks and stress tests find beyond-peak behaviour.

items.stem: Throughput stops increasing while latency rises sharply as load grows. What does this indicate?

options.text: A resource has saturated; the system is past the knee of the curve
options.rationale: Correct: flat throughput with rising latency marks resource saturation.

options.text: The test client is too fast
options.rationale: A fast client does not cause server-side saturation symptoms.

options.text: The SLO is set too low
options.rationale: The SLO setting does not change the observed saturation.
The pattern is a real saturation signal, not a metrics artifact.

items.explanation: Correct: flat throughput with climbing latency is the classic signature of a saturated resource.
